idiom_name: module of service functions + transaction.atomic / context-manager unit of work
implementation_notes: The service class is normally replaced by a module of functions (orders/services.py), one per operation, taking its collaborators as parameters, with the transaction boundary supplied by a context manager: Django's transaction.atomic (which commits on normal exit and rolls back on any exception) or a hand-written @contextmanager unit of work over the session. Nothing in the standard library supplies the layer itself, which is why the structure is a project convention; the class form survives where a service carries state (an API client, a session) or where several services share a base with helpers. A framework provides the transaction half only.
code_sketch:
# orders/services.py
def place_order(*, customer_id: int, items: list[Item], mail: MailGateway) -> int:
    with transaction.atomic():            # commit on exit, rollback on exception
        order = Order.objects.create(customer_id=customer_id)
        for item in items:
            reserve_stock(order, item)    # domain helper, same transaction
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: mail.send_confirmation(order.pk))
        return order.pk
pitfalls: Catching an exception inside atomic() hides the failure from Django and the block then commits - wrap try/except around the atomic block, not inside it.
Autocommit is the default: a service that forgets atomic() leaves every ORM write as its own transaction.
A module-level session or Service instance shared across threads overlaps transactions; keep the unit of work per request.
